utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. There were a few preliminary matters to be raised. Prosecution first. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Regarding your question yesterday about 65 ter 17 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't call you yesterday. I thought that would be inappropriate but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We're starting off -- can I come back in? Thank you for that. There was a 12 June document by General Mladic that made reference to an agreement of -- on June 4th about perhaps transport of supplies to the enclave and other issues. You asked us to see if we could find evidence of such an agreement. We did find about four documents that suggest an agreement and some results of that. We've sent the documents to the Defence last night, and we were just talking. We could provide them in a bar table, we could go over them, we could surprise Mr. Butler with them. A couple of them are on areas that I was planning on going through re-direct with Mr. Butler. So we're at your disposal for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, do you have any views on whether and how they could be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe Mr. McCloskey has re-capsulated [sic] what we discussed, the four documents that we could do them as an agreed bar table at the end of the evidence of the witness, or a written submission, or however Your Honours decide. They're notes from the 4 June meeting between General Janvier and General Mladic. A 12 June letter from General Mladic and then a portion of -- a translation of the notes of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can also in about a minute give you what it appears to me -- what the information would appear -- or what our argument in the bar table would say as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, there seems to be no disagreement to bar table them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, if you still wish to use them with the witness, you have an opportunity to do so. So we'll wait with the bar table until the end of the examination, and then we'll see whether it's just bar tabling them or whether you pay any attention to it. We don't know yet the content. We leave it in your hands at this moment. Then we'll further hear from you. Mr. Ivetic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, D00361 was marked for identification. The B/C/S has been located -- oops, I'm sorry, the translation has been located it is in e-court as 0449-7473-0449-7473-ET. I would ask that it be linked with the original B/C/S and that that document then be admitted as a normal or a regular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was the lack of a translation the only reason to oppose admission? Or were there more reasons?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think it was, but if I can ask my colleagues. I believe that was the Birac Brigade report about the fuel levels in the vehicles, if I'm not mistaken, that for which we did not have the translation, we just had the B/C/S of -- if my recollection is accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is just that problem, then we could resolve it right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, no problem -- no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem. Madam Registrar, you are instructed to attach the English translation just mentioned by Mr. Ivetic to the original B/C/S version of D361. D361 admitted into evidence. Any other matter? If not, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the time to put on the record that the Chamber, on the 3rd of September of this year, has informally granted a Prosecution request to use a comment chart with Witness Milovanovic. And there was another matter, we are still waiting for a response follow-up on what we discussed last Friday, that is, that the Chamber admitted portions of a prior testimony of Witness Music. The Prosecution sent an informal communication requesting leave to add approximately 11 lines, those being page 12.832, line 21, until 20.833, line 6. And we are still waiting whether the Defence objects that addition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, when I -- yes, it should be -- I don't know whether I misread, but the last one should be 12.833. Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I would like to remind you again that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Ivetic will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to start off by talking about a military doctrine known as the "overwhelming force doctrine." Are you familiar with that doctrine, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I'm familiar with the idea. I don't know if I've heard it as the "overwhelming force doctrine", but I believe I know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me see if we have the same definition. The doctrine I'm talking about has the aim to apply massive or overwhelming force as quickly as possible upon an adversary in order to disarm, incapacitate, or render the enemy militarily impotent with as few casualties and losses to our own forces and to non-combatants as possible. Is that the doctrine that you were thinking about that you weren't sure whether it was called overwhelming force?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I'm familiar with the general idea, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is such a doctrine taught and used by the US army and its ally forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would suggest to you that most military forces have at least some variation of this type of doctrine, or at least a tactic as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could a layperson, without military background and training, inartfully and inaccurately describe the application of tactics similar to these as "making the conditions for the enemy's life unbearable"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would suggest that certainly the phrase "making the conditions for the enemy's life unbearable" could, as an isolated phrase, be taken as hyperbole by somebody without a military background, without understanding the broader context of where it is delivered in.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to briefly discuss with you some aspects of the former SFRY military doctrine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A layperson, not familiar with matters, could do anything. Apparently what you are trying to bring to our attention through this witness, is that when those words were used that it may have been the expression of the person using those words, either in writing or in speech, that he may have made that error. That is what you are suggesting, I take it, rather than to keep it all in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because a layperson can misinterpret, can talk rubbish on anything he doesn't have any knowledge about. So therefore if that is what you want to bring to our attention, then don't keep it in the abstract. Focus on what someone said, then of course you can find out whether he was a layperson, whether he had specific knowledge of circumstances, and we get to the core of the issue. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I was talking about directive 7. Did you understand it that way in my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, if he's talking about directive 7, it would be best to read it because that's not the wording of directive 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, are you -- when you were talking about directive 7 and if there's any suggestion that you misquoted it, would you please be so kind to literally quote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, as my question perhaps demonstrated, I wasn't quoting directly from the document. I don't have the exact language before me. But if we -- let's pull it up. Let's go this way. One moment, please. I believe it's P1469. And perhaps counsel can assist with the page number for the text that you wanted quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's in the Drina Corps section. I don't recall what page. I should be able to recite but I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page then. And the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's near the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can go from the back and work our way backwards then. I believe two pages back. What I suggest is -- it's not this page. I suggest we leave this for the break and I'll find the exact page references without spending time on that we can move on to other topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's on the screen now. We just found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ah, there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, reading the text that's before you, I repeat my question: Could this, in your opinion, be a layperson, in-artfully, describing a tactic similar to the overwhelming force tactic that we just discussed and that which is taught -- or that you said most militaries have a similar tactic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again taking into -- directive 7. Colonel Miletic, who drafted this document, is not a layperson. He is, at this time, a senior colonel in the VRS, who shortly thereafter becomes a general or at least a major-general. He is the chief of operations for the VRS Main Staff. That is not a definition of a layperson.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is Mr. Karadzic a definition of a layperson for you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether he has a military background or not, one has to accept that by 1995 he has been the supreme commander of the VRS for three years in combat, he has military advisors, both the Main Staff as well as other military advisors. He's not, you know, he's not a military officer per se, but I don't know that I would call him a layperson any more than I would call the president of the United States a layperson in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And yet directive 7.1 was required after 7.0?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was published after 7.0 as a more technically oriented document for the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And doesn't that, by its virtue, mean that the original document had some layperson terms and was not adequate for the technical orientation -- operation of the military?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, as I've testified before 7/1 supplements directive 7 and it is more focused towards concrete military tasks. I mean, the language here, you know, "by planned and well thought out combat operations ..." and then it goes on to "create unbearable situation," that needs to be turned into a military task. You know, when one looks at a doctrinal book, armies are taught to attack, defend, delay, conduct ambushes. There's not a chapter on how to make an unbearable situation. That larger objective needs to be taken and given in more concrete tasks to the military units that have to carry out that goal. That's what I mean in the sense of taking it and making it more technical in nature for the units that have to carry it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm if your review of the Yugoslav JNA military yielded any documentation or information --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can -- sir, you might want to check on your client. I don't know that he's feeling particularly good this second. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm told that we can proceed. Thank you, sir. Can you confirm if your review of the Yugoslav JNA military yielded any documentation or information that the doctrine of All People's Defence foresaw that "cities were to be defended to the last resident"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, when I looked at my -- or and I looked at the JNA military doctrine, obviously there is a large body of discussion with respect to defence of an urban area, but I don't think I ever came across the phrase that "cities were to be defended to the last resident."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. If we can call up 1D01235 in e-court. And while we wait for that I can tell you this is a decree on the force of law of defence published by the BiH Presidency in the Official Gazette in the Republic of BiH 20 May 1992. And if I can have Article 51 of the same which is found at page 18 in the English, page 3 in the B/C/S. And we'll see here it reads: "All citizens between 15 and 60 (men) or 55 (women) have the right and obligation to train for defence, if fit to attend training. Exemptions are pregnant women, mothers of children below the age of seven and persons declared unfit for training. "The Government shall issue regulations for pertinent reimbursements." At the time of doing your research and analysing the events, were you familiar with such a provision being effective and in existence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again I didn't do too much research on the ABiH military doctrine, but certainly this language is consistent with the same language that I've seen on the VRS side or on the RS side. It was a standard staple of mandatory military service that all three sides took from the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can continue with this theme, I'd like to re-visit some matters from the Popovic case, 1D1246. And if we can please have page 55 in e-court which should correlate to transcript page 20.559 in that case's transcript. And actually, I apologise. It would be the next -- the next page, page 56, which would be transcript page 20.560, if we can look at line 8. And you're talking about the SFRY All People's Defence in this section. And it reads as follows: "Q. The basis of this concept for the society in former Yugoslavia, which was based on self-management, the basis of the concept of All People's Defence was that someone -- that everybody should take part, in one way or another, to defence? "A. Yes, ma'am. I mean, it's a reflection of the -- one, the past history of the former Yugoslavia under occupation during World War II, and also a reflection of their modern defence strategy, which called for a situation where, if invaded by either the NATO Bloc or the Warsaw Bloc, you know, recognising they didn't have the military force to forestall that invasion, they would adopt a strategy of insurgent warfare within their own country as a way of making a foreign occupation so expensive that an opponent would ultimately leave. So, you know, in that context, that is what All People's Defence resolved around, the fact that not only all individuals but all sectors of the Yugoslav state would be part of that defence." Is this part of your testimony in Popovic case accurate to your recollections about this topic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, when talking about these directives that were written, and in particular let's focus on directive 4 with you, do you agree that when these were drafted they would have been drafted by persons that -- that had this doctrine or background of the former SFRY that all sides adopted in mind and that it has to be understood within that context?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, as I testified last week when somebody asked me the exact same question, clearly the people who drafted directive 4 in that context, you know, understood that the ABiH military forces that were in East Bosnia would draw support from the local Bosnian Muslim population that was there, just like the VRS officers who were former JNA were trained in that doctrine, certainly the ABiH officers were as well. I mean, so both sides had an understanding of what would be counter-insurgency warfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to explore with you demilitarisation of the enclave of Srebrenica. You testified, in your direct, that General Morillon unilaterally declared Srebrenica a safe area, and am I correct that this occurred after the Sarajevo authorities of the BiH forbade the UN-sponsored evacuation of civilians from Srebrenica in 1993?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the timing, which came first. I can tell you that you are obviously correct that the UN was at a point in time removing civilians from the encircled area, and that at a point in time, the ABiH stopped them from doing that. I think it was that that predicated the UN Security Council declaring or formalising it a safe area, but I -- I just -- it's been a while since I've looked at that component so I can't give you the exact dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: From your -- from your perspective as a military man, was the prohibition issued by the Sarajevo authorities preventing the further evacuation of civilians from Srebrenica in accord with their obligations, especially under Article 17 of Geneva Conventions 4 and the Additional Protocols like Article 51 in relation to precautionary measures of a defending military force?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that the ABiH and even to some degree the United Nations' perspective was that by evacuating the population, that they were becoming complicit in an ethnic cleansing campaign. Having said that, as I military professional, now my view was: I would have liked to see the civilians out of there had I been given a choice or a vote on that one. Getting the civilians out of that particular scenario, in my mind should have overrode a decision as to whether or not they're complicit in ethnic cleansing. Once you get them out of that there, you can have that argument. Using them in that particular context, again, if I had a vote, I wouldn't have voted to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could briefly take a look at Exhibit P23. This is a demilitarisation agreement dated 8 May 1993. I first want to know when it comes up. Are you familiar with this document from your research and did you review it at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In that case, if we can turn to the last page, and it is signed by the most senior military officers of both the VRS and by the ABiH on the one hand, and also signed by General Morillon. Based on your knowledge of military law, international law, are parties able to conclude binding local agreements to declare areas demilitarised zones where military activity will not take place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they can.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you consider insofar as the ABiH did not demilitarise the area as per the prior agreement, that military actions in 1993 of the VRS were justified?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to Srebrenica, I believe I've been consistent that because the -- what was first OG8, Operational Group 8, and then later the 28th Division, was never fully disarmed and, in fact, I believe that the historical record will note that it continued to conduct military operations throughout the period, I've always testified that I believed that that represented a lawful object of attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I'd like to put some specifics to this, if we can look at 1D1249 in e-court. Once we get that up I think we'll see it's dated the 20th of April, 1993, from General Halilovic of the ABiH. And now that we have the English on the screen, could you take a look at it and see if you believe you would have had an opportunity to review this document in the course of your work?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I would have looked at this document in detail for my reports, but certainly I have seen it and I believe in some context I've testified about it several times since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about the first part of this, the first paragraph that reads: "We hereby inform you that no meaningful progress was made in the negotiations on the demilitarisation of Srebrenica held on 19 April 1993. It was specified that the aggressor, regardless of the contents of the already signed agreement on demilitarisation of Srebrenica town, insisted that all units at defence lines surrender their weapons, thus demilitarising the area as they see it, which would be separated by a line of disengagement." Now, I'd like to ask you this interpretation of demilitarisation that Mr. Halilovic's aggressor is -- the person he terms as aggressor, is advocating, is that not in fact precisely what is meant by the term from your military background?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I'm not sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Neither does at least some of the Judges, so could you please rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This interpretation of "demilitarisation," the part that the aggressor -- he says the aggressor's insisting on that all units at defence lines surrender their weapons, thus demilitarising the areas as they see it, which would then be separated by a line of disengagement. Isn't that precisely a key aspect of the concept of a demilitarised zone, as you understand it, as a military analyst?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess looking at this context, the discussion was over whether or not it was simply the town of Srebrenica that was demilitarised or the surrounding area which the army still occupied. And again, that is one of the -- the broader issues that was discussed. I mean, one would think in a larger demilitarised zone it would mean just that. Military troops, if you're in a demilitarised zone, you're not supposed to be carrying weapons and things of that nature beyond, you know, maybe side-arms for select cases of self-defence. So, I think that's what the context of this first paragraph is discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, just for my understanding, do I understand you to be asking whether insisting on surrender of weapons is the same thing as demilitarisation by agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, my question was specifically as to the concept of a demilitarised zone as understood under military law. I believe it's an international -- internationally recognised concept, and that this was part of the definition, whereas Mr. Halilovic is claiming that the aggressor, the other side, is insisting upon this in error as my reading this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Butler can assist us. Is it correct when using the term "aggressor," the ABiH is usually referring to the -- is referring to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is correct. I mean, when they use the phrase "aggressor," they refer to the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Does that address Your Honour's question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It does not, but you may carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at the next part.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "UNPROFOR's view of demilitarisation, which is fully supported by us, is full demilitarisation of Srebrenica and a small area around it, visible to the naked eye, where the only armed persons would be the civilian police. Therefore, it is necessary to pull out all armed persons, soldiers, and reserve policemen and reinforce defence lines to the maximum. We are fully supported in this by Morillon and Wahlgren and the entire international public (community)." Is this idea of having Srebrenica appear demilitarised to the naked eye but having defence lines reinforced to the maximum, consistent with the spirit of demilitarised zones under international law on the one hand? Let's ask that first, sir.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm not an international law expert. I mean, I can see obviously where the ABiH would draw a military advantage if this was the scenario, but again, as you indicated in your earlier testimony, the warring parties or the leaders of the warring parties, you know, are obviously able to conclude any type of agreement, in this respect, that they want. So again, I mean, that's, you know, they can do whatever they want on this but, you know, from my perspective, I mean, you can clearly see where the ABiH would enjoy a military advantage here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And having studied the demilitarised agreement that eventually was reached or were reached, would this description, by General Halilovic, be consistent with the spirit and letter of those agreements?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the 28th Division and OG8 never fully disarmed throughout the territory. So whether or not they were consistent with the spirit of the agreement or not, you know, I'm not sure I'm the best person to say that. But I can tell you that from an objective perspective, you know, the OG8, and then later the 28th Infantry Division, did conduct military activities and they were conducting those activities armed. So they did not behave in a demilitarised manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One last part I would ask your assistance to analyse -- the last paragraph of this document which is: "We need to fortify defence lines and urgently send a kurban," and the translator's note that this is a sacrifice or a victim, "to Naser. The disarmament of our troops is out of the question - not a single soldier, much less a whole unit. The 2nd Corps Command has to find a way to send the kurban." Did your research reveal what sacrifice, or victim, the ABiH was planning for Srebrenica's military forces to give Naser Oric already in 1993?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't know what that phrase means.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, can we tender this as the next available exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I see in English on page 1 that there's handwriting on the handwritten 178. In the original, however, I see that there's more handwriting there --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do see that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which seems not to be translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree and I just noticed on the bottom left there is some handwriting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that is translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think yes, that seems to be translated. Any idea what that is so we could ask for? I mean if it's just -- if you have any idea on what it might mean then -- or if Mr. McCloskey would have any idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe the first word is "cuvati," which would be "to keep" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, it would be perhaps an instruction where to store the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the understanding of the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm told by Mr. Lukic it means to keep -- I guess to store and keep in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which we should probably get the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we do not know who wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems not of vital importance for the understanding and for the testimony about this document. So therefore, although I'm usually not very much inclined to accept documents which are not fully translated, at the same time I would have to consult with my colleagues whether we do have to insist on a further translation. It seems we do not insist. Therefore, Madam Registrar, the number would be ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D01249 receives number D366, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I next want to look at 65 ter number 17957. And in relation to this document, it's dated 21 May 1993 and is, again, from the ABiH side of things, this time in relation to Zepa. And I think you can see the first part indicates: "Pursuant to the authorisation of the SVK," and the translator says "Supreme Command Staff R BH OS, confidential number 02/639-3 dated 20 May 1993, the plan to demilitarise Zepa was inspected by an officer of the Army of the Republic of BH and an officer of the aggressor, as organised by UNPROFOR. "The opinions, views and conclusions are as follows ..." And then we see there that UNPROFOR representative Mr. Valentine was the UNPROFOR individual for this and he has some conclusions that are numbered as 1 through 6. I would like to look at 1 through 3 with you. They read as follows: "1) that UNPROFOR has fully complied with Articles 1, 2, and 5 of the Agreement; "2) that the Serb side has complied with its duties in the Agreement in sequence; "3) that our side has not complied with Article 3 and that UNPROFOR does not want a museum in Zepa, referring to the content and type of weapons that were handed over ..." Did you have this document, or this type of information, available to you that the Serb side was deemed to have complied with its duties under the agreement, whereas the ABiH side had not and attempted to pass off pieces that were described as belonging in a museum, as the weapons that they were handing over?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, in the context of both Zepa and Srebrenica, many of the weapons that the ABiH did hand over as part of the demilitarisation were considered to be obsolete or inoperable. So they had very little military value anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this document, but I see we don't have the B/C/S original. So I propose we MFI the same and hopefully the Prosecution can provide the original, as it is their document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection. I'm sure we can find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 17957 receives number D367, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to take a look together at 1D00882. While we wait for that, I can introduce it as being dated 11 August 1995 by a Mr. Ramiz Becirovic, who is said to be the Chief of Staff of the ABiH forces in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the record this is Exhibit D270.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look at the first few lines of this, I think it's something that you probably have seen before, but there is the use of the term "Chetnik" to describe Serbs. Based on your research, was that intended to be a derogatory term meant to dehumanise the enemy?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it certainly was a derogatory term.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree that the term was used consistently by both the head of the ABiH party and the political leadership of the BiH, both in official written documents as well as in TV and newspaper publications?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I've never studied that particular issue, so I don't know if I can give you an informed comment of how consistently it was used by those individuals. I can say that, you know, it was a common -- certainly among ABiH documents and things that I've read.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we can turn to page 2 in both the English and the B/C/S of this document and if we can focused on the bottom of the page in the English and it starts off there, sir: "It was very difficult to organise joint logistical support, since every local community had its own logistics and fed its army. We tried to agree that when a Serbian village was liberated, the entire booty would be directed to joint warehouses and then be divided into equal parts. However, as soon as a village was liberated, the people would rush in and everyone took what he wanted. As a result, further attempts to establish joint logistics were abandoned." Sir, does this provide an example of the civilian population taking part in hostilities and supporting the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where does it talk about the civilian population, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "Every local community had its own logistics and fed its army."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could that be more specific? I thought he was referring to the part about the people rushing in, and Mr. Butler needs to know what he's talking about with this because -- as opposed to free question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, what part have I not read to? I thought I gave him the whole paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently the way in which Judge Moloto understood the question and Mr. McCloskey understood the question was that you referred to the latter part of the portion you read and not at the beginning part. That seems to have created some confusion. Could you be as specific as possible, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The reference to "every local community had its own logistics and fed its army," could that be understood as an example of the civilian population taking part in hostilities and supporting the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we split that up in one, taking part in hostilities --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and second supporting the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and that was the point I was going to make. Certainly the local population did support the ABiH forces in a rather decentralised manner in that area. So they did provide food, shelter, and what they could to the army. Again, doing that doesn't necessarily mean that they're participating in hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now let me focus on the second part of this that's on the next page in the English. In relation to the statement here that as soon as a village was liberated, the people would rush in and everyone took what he wanted, did you, in the course of your research, discover whether that included civilians?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did. I mean, again looking at the context of what was happening there during the winter of 1992 and 1993, you know, they were deep within occupied territory and it doesn't surprise me that when they would take a village over, that they would try and strip it of everything they could use, both the military and the surrounding civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in your opinion, would that be the civilians taking part in hostilities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't -- I wouldn't frame it as such, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we can turn to page 5 of the English, page 4 of the B/C/S, it's the second full paragraph in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my understanding, Mr. Ivetic, otherwise I might miss the gist of your questions. The people, including civilians, rushing in and taking whatever he wanted, let's say someone takes their window-frame or a door or a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: TV --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or a TV or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- I think in their context, it would be food primarily, they didn't have electricity out there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but they might have expected to have electricity once again. I mean, is it your suggestion that that -- that that is the type of activity which would become taking part in hostilities or even supporting the army? Because you could also -- taking whatever you want, if the army wants to keep everything together and use it in an organised way, could also be understood as undermining the activities of the army. That came to my mind, and therefore I was wondering how you read this and whether it would -- how it would be to take part in hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think the analysis would have to look at the specific facts, and that therefore more analysis would be required than to make a full appraisal of the actions just based upon a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you asked it on the basis of this text; that's exactly my concern, Mr. Ivetic. When I now say: How do we then have to understand this? You say, well, we need more facts, but you asked the question without reference to any facts, just on the basis of this text. Let's leave it to that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can focus on the second full paragraph that is on the page before us. It says: "After we got those two agreements on the demilitarisation of Srebrenica, we had to disarm completely. We barely managed to secure some older weapons in disrepair to hand over to UNPROFOR while the troops hid the rest at their homes." First of all, sir, in your opinion was there an organised intent on the part of the ABiH to deceive the international community that it had demilitarised, since we now see similar tactics in both Srebrenica and Zepa as to the handing over of older weapons subsequent to the signing of the demilitarisation agreements?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this comment that the troops hid the rest of the weapons at their homes, what would be the effect of taking weapons and introducing them into a civilian dwelling? Would that dwelling retain its civilian status according to your understanding of military doctrine and international law?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of all of the things that are going to be a fact-by-fact analysis, whether or not taking a weapon into a civilian dwelling, I mean one weapon or 50 or a hundred makes that suddenly now a legitimate object of attack, again it's going to have to be on the specifics. Again, the analogy I keep in mind on this is that clearly, you know, people working in a military hospital are armed for self protection and, you know, because they're also storing weapons there for soldiers who come in for treatment. The mere possession of those weapons in a military hospital does not make it a military object of attack. I don't know, you know, like I said, does one weapon in a civilian house make it an object of attack, I would doubt it. Would a hundred? That might be different under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see we're at the time for the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's time for the first break. Could you give us an indication, Mr. Ivetic, how much time you would still need. And the witness can meanwhile leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: A little more than an hour, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Little more than an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, any news from the Defence already on adding to the 92 bis portion of -- in relation to Witness Music?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm told -- one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm told we're still collecting the transcript pages to have them reviewed by our staff in the back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll wait for further messages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we do have a B/C/S of D00367, which was the MFI number. It's doc ID 01857879-0.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that you would like to have it attached to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please attach the document just referred to by Mr. McCloskey to D367. Once it is done, it can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, just before the break and I think at least once before in your answers you have sought to draw the analogy to a hospital and have given your testimony about that. Would you agree with me, sir, that hospitals have a separate definition from other civilian structures and that is pursuant to Article 22 of the first Geneva Conventions, and thus an analogy between a hospital and any other civilian structure, that depending on the circumstances may be converted to a military purpose, is inapplicable?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mean to compare them in the technical sense like that. It was simply trying to explain in a broader sense the analogy -- maybe a better analogy, for example, would be what happens or what happened, you know, in Iraq when military forces would go in and search homes. The fact that they would find a weapon from an insurgent in a home did not make the home a military object subject to destruction. On the other hand, if people were firing at military troops from that home, that home would become part of a military object, it being used for a military purpose, and thus it would be potentially subject to destruction. So again, that's why I go back to, you know, it would -- at what point in time -- getting to your broader question, at what point in time civilian population or civilian objects lose their protection and become the object, or at least, potentially subject to attack by a military force, is a very fact-specific exercise that has to be looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to move to another document, but before I do, do you believe that the UNPROFOR sent a sufficient number of forces to the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa in order to permit them to fulfil their task of demilitarising those areas?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe the UN ever believed that they had enough people. The UN report notes the fact that they actually did come up with a figure of how many people they would need to enforce that, and I believe the UN's own report discusses that they could not find countries willing to put the troops in there to do that. I mean, the consequence is obviously that, no, the UN never have enough troops to fulfil their mandates there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now if we can look at 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You included in your question, and I don't know whether exactly the witness has observed that, that the demilitarisation was the task of UNPROFOR, which of course is something I don't know whether you noticed that, that that was part of Mr. Ivetic's question. And therefore the question is: Do you consider that demilitarising Srebrenica and Zepa was the task or responsibility or that the UNPROFOR play a role and what role. Did you intend by saying -- by answering that question, did you include an admission of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect to UNPROFOR, one of their concrete roles was to guard the weapons that had been turned in. Another role that they had was to essentially maintain a perimeter around the enclave to prevent military activity going on, military forces, from the ABiH passing through to attack the Serbs, Serbs passing through to attack the Muslims. They never had enough personnel to do that. And again, going back to the UN's own report, the UN itself, as a body and consequently UNPROFOR, was very ambiguous about whether their mandate actually included enforcing a demilitarised zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it was not -- it was part of the question and by answering the question you did not specifically address to what extent it was the task of UNPROFOR to demilitarise. Mr. Ivetic, we have heard a lot of evidence on that. I think we have looked in detail about the -- all the texts that cover that, so therefore I'm not seeking to re-visit all that but just to make clear that in your question you should avoid to include matters which may not be properly observed by the witness in preparing his answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we can look at 65 ter 1D01236.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait for that, I can introduce it to you, sir, this is a list of some 27 pages in the English of combat operations carried out within the 2nd Corps zone of responsibility by the ABiH and signed by General Delic during the time-period of 1992 through 1995. First of all, sir, would this zone include the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you see, or do you believe, that you had access to this report at the time that you were doing your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I've seen this document before, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we could turn to page 12 in the B/C/S and page 18 of the same in English. Based upon the dates, going in sequential order, I believe this is where we start with the activities subsequent to the demilitarisation agreements. If we start with 2 June 1993, which is number 428 on the list, and if we go through the entirety of the list -- or, excuse me, not through the entirety of the list, but if we go all the way through June 1995, which is number 633 on the list, it would appear that the ABiH admits to undertaking 205 combat actions during that same time-period before the VRS executed the Krivaja 95 operation. Does that figure accord with your review and research?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and could Mr. Butler be given a bit of time to review that. He would also, I think, need a map to determine if any of these villages are in the enclave. Because I don't see how it's relevant if we're talking about all 2nd Corps action all up and down the defence line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we could give some additional time and would you --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure, I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- give a map -- I don't know exactly what -- what the relevance and what you want to establish through these questions but --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I simply want to find out whether, in his review, if the entirety of the actions in this zone of responsibility are encapsulated by this document which he says he did not see. So I'm trying to see whether he had knowledge, even though he didn't see the document, of the facts contained therein, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore the witness would have to look at the whole of the list in detail and see -- then tell us whether they're all in here, but that makes sense only if the witness claims to have knowledge of all this type of --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- this text of this because otherwise he couldn't tell us whether it's complete or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right and that's why I was asking if he had that information. If he does then he would have to look at the list and if he does not then it's a moot point and we move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you be able to see whether this list is complete after you would have taken your time to -- if you would have had an opportunity to know exactly where it all is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have only one page of this list on the screen in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And there are 27 pages. Witness, do you think you could do that at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not over a 20-minute break, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I do understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is feasible, obviously, with the time and, you know, the necessary resources for me to go over this list and to at least identify which of these combat actions are directly related to, or could potentially be related to, Srebrenica and Zepa. It would -- again, it would take me some time, but it is something I could accomplish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What means "some time" for you in this respect for 27 pages of this kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably -- I could do it probably inside a week, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That -- Mr. Ivetic, I leave it in your hands -- well, first of all, of course we -- before a witness comes in and then is tasked with a job of a week, that would need more than just a request from the Defence. I wonder, Mr. Ivetic, what purpose it would finally serve --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- finding out what the witness knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think again, if we get back to my question: Did he have knowledge of military actions undertaken by the 2nd Corps within the zone of responsibility during the time-period between the demilitarisation agreement and the end of 1995. If he says he had that in mind when he did his analysis, it's a fruitful effort; if he says he did not have that in mind, then it's not -- and we don't gain anything by having his analyse the 27 pages to see which ones relate to the enclave. So again I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, your question was -- you took the witness, I think, to a certain date and a number on the list and then your question was -- you said: It would appear that the ABiH admits to undertake 205 combat actions during that same time-period and whether that does -- that figure accord with your review and research? I do now understand that the simple answer is no because you never analysed this, although, and that may be the question Mr. Ivetic would like to put to you, is whether a number of 200 combat actions after a certain point in time, whether that is more or less consistent with the overall impression you have gained from your research?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that would -- that would be my answer. I mean, as I've testified before -- I mean, with respect to the 28th Division and OG8, they did conduct military operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether the number of 215 with 2nd Corps matters or not, I mean I -- from a military perspective, I mean obviously I'm aware in broad sense, the military operations and I do take that into account in my reports. I -- so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They were not rare, they happened with certain frequency. But my first question would be: Apart from 205, I never noticed that there's a great dispute about the 28th Division engaging in all kind of military actions during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I haven't seen any yet. Mr. Butler, is the foundation of the Prosecution's case that, from his reports and his testimonies he lays it out. And my objection to this would be the relevance of 2nd Corps. He's talking 2nd Corps, not 28th -- 28th Division is inside the enclave. 2nd Corps is -- there's a very long front line and Mr. Butler may know it better than I do. But the actions along that entire front line, I don't see how that gets to be relevant --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- to our case and this first page, I don't recognise any of the villages inside the enclave or outside the enclave on this page. And I think -- my guess is Mr. Ivetic and I can agree, looking at this list, which of these are inside or immediately outside of the enclave and probably just as well as Mr. Butler can.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's probably true --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say you would do the job which would take Mr. Butler approximately a week. Okay, there's an offer -- there seems to be an agreement. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If -- if we can look at one -- pardon me, Exhibit D17. And while we wait for that, sir, this is a document dated the 30th of June, 1995, and I think we'll see it's for the command of the 28th Division of the ABiH in Srebrenica. And I can tell you that the signature on the next page is Mr. Becirovic, the Chief of Staff, whom we have discussed before. I would like to focus first on item number -- well, the first part, the results that have been achieved during this one operation report, 13 Chetniks killed and I think you testified about this in another case, that you can't tell whether the Chetniks that are mentioned here would include civilians or be limited to military personnel. Am I -- is my recollection correct about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe that I discussed this document at length in the Tolimir case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we see the next part in item number 2 it says: "In order to prevent enemy forces from sending additional forces from the Srebrenica and Zepa areas to the Sarajevo theatre, two acts of sabotage were carried out near Srebrenica - on 23 June 1995 at Osmace and on 23 June 1995 in Bijela Stijena near Koprivno, and the following results achieved ..." And then it lists them. The question that I have for you, first of all, are these activities consistent with your investigation, that is, that often times the military actions of the 28th Division were intended to divert the VRS from sending their troops to respond to attacks by other ABiH units including the 2nd Corps within its zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, many of the attacks that the 28th Division undertook were specifically designed to keep the VRS military forces surrounding the enclave as opposed to being sent to other places on the battle-field where they might play a big role. It could be 2nd Corps in this particular case talking about the Sarajevo theatre you're talking about ABiH 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And as a military analyst, would you agree, since we see items number 3 and 4 on this same document if we scroll down, also talking about diverting the enemy forces from the Sarajevo theatre towards -- by conducting attacks surrounding Srebrenica, that in fact the VRS's focus on the Srebrenica region was intended by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is your question -- did the ABiH conduct military operations, one of the primary purposes being to tie-down forces around Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can now look at 1D1271. This is a coded cable from the United Nations. If we could turn to page 2 of the same, I'd like to ask you about item number 3 "restrictions on movement BSA liaison officers." And it says: "The BH, the BiH has imposed numerous restrictions on movement (ROM) on UNPROFOR. The historical trend is that ROM are levied wherever the BH, BiH is undertaking military activity or attempting to pressure UNPROFOR. Over the past two months, the BiH has applied ROM in Sector North East and South West and presumably to screen their military activities, and also to force the withdrawal of the BSA liaison officers from Tuzla and Gornji Vakuf." First of all sir, is the area know as Sector North East that is discussed here, an area that includes the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you should really slow down while reading and take into account, please, everything has to be translated into French.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise and I will try to address that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at item (a) under this topic, dealing with regard to Sector North East. "In January 1995, the BiH imposed a blockade of Sector North East to protest the presence of the BSA LO at Tuzla Air Base (TAB). Access was restricted to HQ Sector North East stationed the TAB, as well as to several company locations and resupply into several observation posts (OPs). Following the departure of the BSA LO, restrictions were slowly, but not completely, lifted. OPs in the northern region of the Sector, as well as UNPROFOR movement in the Sapna Thumb and the west of the Srebrenica enclave, are the subject of restrictions imposed by the BiH. Concurrently, an unprecedented number of BiH fuel and supply convoys have been seen moving into the northern region of the Sector." Now, first of all, sir, this reference to fuel and -- BiH fuel and supply convoys that are seen in this region, would you expect that we are talking about military or civilian convoys?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expect that, in the context of this discussion, that we would be talking about materiels for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information about this time-period from which you would be able to give us more specifics as to the -- these activities and the types of convoys? Or the numbers of convoys I should say?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document as an exhibit at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D01271 receives number D368, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D368 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, if we can turn to page 4 of this document, one more item I'd like to discuss with you, sir, to see if you had this in mind. It is at the bottom of the page and begins with the line "thirdly" and reads as follows: "Thirdly, the government's actions are designed in part to convince the international community that the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement is not working, with the aim of discrediting the Bosnian Serbs. In fact, it is the Bosnian Government which is proving the more difficult by imposing new restrictions on freedom of movement and refusing to attend Joint Commission meetings. As a result UNPROFOR is in a position of stalemate" if we can go to the next page "and problems cannot be properly addressed through the Joint Commission process. Serb restrictions, on the other hand, have eased considerably, although tight controls are still imposed on fuel deliveries to the enclave. It must, however, be kept in mind that UNPROFOR has no access to Serb-controlled areas, and that military observers have not returned to the Brcko corridor." Now, this information here from the beginning of 1995 that paints a picture that while the Serb side was relaxing its restrictions, the BiH was, in fact, the party working against the agreements in place. Did you have such information, and take into account such information, in the process of doing your work?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've -- I have seen this document, obviously. I was aware of the broader context when I was writing my reports, and in fact, you know, as part of the historical overview of my narrative report I indicate the fact that the VRS was growing aware that, you know, 1995 was going to be a year of decision, at least with respect to the military framework. They understood that at some point the ABiH was going to abandon the cease-fire, just like they also understood that down the line that the Republic of Croatia was going to re-enter the war to a large degree. So clearly, you know, to make those observations I had to have some understanding of what was happening in January of 1995, and again this document paints an accurate picture of the UN's perception of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I'd like to move again back to the time-period just before the Srebrenica Krivaja operation. Did you know that on the 12th of May, 1995, General Manojlo Milovanovic went into the field in the Drina Corps area to examine the activities in that area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have. I don't recall at the moment. It may have been something I looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to 1D1246 and page 32 of the same, which should correlate to transcript page 20.536 of the Popovic transcripts. And I would like to focus on line 20 and thereon. It reads as follows, sir: "My question is this: On the 12th of May, 1995" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you made it a -- more or less a habit to read all the portions of documents and transcripts, where the witness could read it for himself, which takes a third of the time, and then you ask a focused question. And then, if the documents or the transcript is then exhibited, then we can move on. Could you please try to see whether it is really necessary to read such long portions and where you can do without.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can direct your attention, sir, to lines 20 through 23, does that refresh your recollection whether or not you had knowledge of General Milovanovic's visiting the Drina Corps area in -- on the 12th of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. From my answer, I take it I did not have knowledge of that event when she asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree that in times of absence by General Mladic, General Milovanovic would have been in a de jure role as deputy commander of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: By virtue of the regulations and the organisation of the Main Staff, if General Mladic is absent or otherwise unable to exercise command of the Main Staff, his deputy, General Milovanovic, would have taken that role, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that that -- that there was no separate or specific order required for General Milovanovic to fulfil that role, that it would be an automated process?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't disagree that it -- that he would need a formal order to do that. I do disagree that it's an automated process. Obviously, as General Mladic's deputy, General Milovanovic is going to be closely engaged with whatever scenario is taking place and he will clearly, you know, again in co-ordination with General Mladic, know under what circumstances he's authorised to take command.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, now we've -- you've testified about your knowledge of the fact that General Mladic left the Srebrenica area and participated in some meetings and other events in Serbia in July of 1995. Would you agree that there would be no need for General Mladic to issue any order for his deputy commander to assume command in his absence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree. I mean, General Mladic -- I mean, if we take -- first of all, if we look at July of 1995, I believe I've already testified that, given the circumstances at the time, General Milovanovic was on the Krajina and that in the absence of General Mladic, if he was unable to take or exercise command, that it would be General Miletic as the chief of operations who would do that. Now -- so in that particular context would whomever was the person who would assume command, if it's General Milovanovic or if it's General Miletic, yes, they would need to co-ordinate with General Mladic in order to know at least what the circumstances are going to be by which he's not able to exercise command. Merely leaving an area or even in the case of General Mladic going across the border to Serbia would not normally create the circumstances by which General Mladic would essentially relinquish command of the VRS. You would have to look at the actual circumstances involved with respect to his ability to exercise command.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you perform an analysis, either in your -- any of your written works how General Mladic's physical absence from the zone of the VRS would be treated under the relevant VRS regulations, rules, and structure?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I looked at that very closely because obviously very early on in the investigation we knew that, one, General Mladic was indicted for Srebrenica already; and two, that we were able to place him in Belgrade on days where components of the crime took place. So we did look very closely at what were the mechanisms with respect to the VRS in the circumstance if General Mladic could not exercise command, who the next responsible people would be. My conclusion in looking at all of the material and as well as various interviews of individuals who were on the Main Staff is that the fact that General Mladic went to Belgrade during those days does not mean that he has relinquished command to anybody. I've not heard testimony from any VRS officer that I recall talking to who has indicated that they were aware that on the 14th and 15th that General Mladic wasn't in command and that command of the VRS had been assumed by either General Milovanovic as the deputy or by General Miletic as the chief of operations. So, I mean, we did look at it. I certainly looked at it, but there's no evidence that would support that theory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, the question was focusing primarily, I think, on relevant VRS regulations, rules, and structure. Now your answer was, I would say, for 90 per cent what happened in fact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, within the regulations, sir, to be clear, it -- simply being out of the zone of responsibility does not automatically create the circumstances by which you can no longer command. And so, I mean, that -- again, there was a regulatory basis for that and that is what we looked at, to see if there was a practical answer to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you perform any factual investigation to ascertain the method of transportation used by General Mladic during his travels and the technical specifications of those transport means, including communications devices available or not, on the same?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did. And again, when I say "we," the broader investigation did. He did travel by automobile. I don't know that I can say that the vehicle that he travelled in had the ability to communicate while he was driving, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to turn back and rewind a bit to the beginning of July 1995 and the Krivaja 95 operation. You in your direct examination have stated that General Mladic or others from the Main Staff were out in the field with the commanders at the corps level and I would -- is it your understanding that they were also out there with commanders of the brigades or battalions directing and commanding directly the actions of these as to the Srebrenica campaign? Am I understanding your evidence to be like that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General -- well, first General Gvero and then General Mladic were located at the IKM forward headquarters of the Drina Corps during the relevant days. There they would have had access to the Drina Corps Chief of Staff and his staff officers and I believe at various times the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, who was also there. Obviously, I believe the Court has seen the 11 July 1995 video where General Mladic and other officers are walking through Srebrenica, where he's addressing the various brigade commanders. But I don't believe that during the run-up from the 10th, when he first arrived, his place would have been at the IKM. He would not have been in the field, sitting behind various brigade or battalion commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you believe that while at the IKM he was able to interject himself and issue commands directly to the subordinate units of the corps or that anyone from the Main Staff could do so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not anyone from the Main Staff could do so, but certainly General Mladic could and I believe that there are several documents I talked about where he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. In this regard, would you agree with the description of the VRS Main Staff as a strategic organ rather than an operational organ?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It -- whether it was designed that way or not, the reality was that it functioned at both the strategic level as well as the operational level. In a perfect world, the VRS would have been simply strategic and dealing with the larger issues of the army. The fact was that it was heavily involved in operations as well, certainly with respect to corps-level operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that, in a traditional sense, a strategic organ would be one that plans actions involving two or more corps and would not be involved in planning operations that are within one corps' zone of operations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir. I mean, and again when you look at the Krivaja 95 operations plan, you see just that. The plan was designed by and authored, essentially, by the Drina Corps and briefed to the Main Staff for their approval. Since almost all of the assets involved in that came from the Drina Corps, there was not necessarily a requirement to co-ordinate with either the neighbouring corps, the Herzegovina Corps or the East Bosnia Corps or the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, for resources or things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could try to understand your testimony where you claim the VRS functioned as both an operational and as a strategic organ. The information that I have is that as of January 1995, the Main Staff was only staffed at 37 per cent of the officers that were foreseen under the establishment, 41 per cent of the necessary junior officers, and 50 per cent of the necessary soldiers or non -- non-officers. In reaching your conclusion, did you have that kind of a picture and that kind of information in mind?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, yes, sir. I mean, while I don't understand -- or I don't recall the specific numbers, and I think I've testified I've never done analysis of the specific numbers, I understand that they were understaffed. My response to that is: So were the corps. So while the manning of the Main Staff was low, the fact is that it was comparable to the staffs of the corps that they were controlling, which is why you see sometimes the Main Staff being involved in lower-level planning or even execution of corps operations because of the recognised deficiency.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I think in my cross you earlier confirmed that none of the orders that you reviewed which originated from General Mladic expressly ordered commission of crimes, and you spent a lot of your time in direct speculating as to the plans and intent of persons based on words and deeds of others. I'd like to look at what --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's argumentative. Had he been speculating, that would have drawn an objection, and I didn't hear any objection to speculation. So those kind of comments are argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could you please put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to focus on what General Mladic is actually recorded as having said at various points. If we could first have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you to put a question to the witness, not to continue argument. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm a bit confused as to what is considered argument out of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we can have 65 ter number 04624.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this will be your corps command responsibility report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can have page 28 of the same. It will be, I believe, two pages forward in the B/C/S, focusing on paragraph 7.4 of your report -- sorry, next page in the B/C/S. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, here you talk of guide-lines for criminal prosecution of offenders that were issued on 6 October 1992 by -- that were forwarded by General Mladic from the VRS military prosecutor's office. First of all, would you agree that these guide-lines forwarded by General Mladic are entirely proper and appropriate from a military aspect, covering all the type of legal prohibitions that you would expect to find in a professional, modern army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, as far as the military courts and military prosecutors are concerned, during the relevant time-period those were under the control of the Ministry of Defence and were not under General Mladic's direct authority. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
