utterances.text: When the conflict began, the military court system was under the jurisdiction of the Main Staff. I believe sometime in the middle of 1993 the Republika Srpska made a decision to transfer the military court system from the Main Staff's jurisdiction to the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen any orders of General Mladic which purport to interfere in the work of the military courts or the military prosecutors as you interpret them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. And in fact, many of the orders that I've seen are from the Main Staff or from corps commanders who are complaining because they want to see a more robust military judiciary and prosecutor's office because they're dealing with a back-log of offences that the courts are unable to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can have D143 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think you'll see this is an 11 July 1995 letter to General Smith of UNPROFOR from General Mladic. I'd like to focus on the first two paragraphs and since we don't have the B/C/S. It says: "I have received your letter from 9 July 1995. The Srebrenica enclave has not been demilitarised according to the agreements of 19 April and 8 May 1993. The Muslims have not handed over the weapons, mine/explosives and combative means to UNPROFOR. The Muslim forces have abused the special status of the safe area and presence of your forces for preparing and performing of terrorist and other fighting activities against Serb population and the territory of the Republic of Srpska. "I remind you that up to now the Muslim forces have killed a hundred and wounded over two hundreds of Serb civilians by their attacks and infiltrated sabotage-terrorist groups. Several Serb villages in the immediate vicinity of the safe area have been burnt down with not yet seen massacres of civilians. Over last few days they have launched an extensive military action with an aim of connecting with the enclave of the village of Zepa, and have burnt the villages of Visnjica and Banja Lucica and killed their inhabitants. Accomplishing their hideous intentions, the Muslims have not spared even the members of UNPROFOR units. In spite of protecting them, your forces have become their victims too." Now, in your review of the events from this time-period, are these words by General Mladic factually accurate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't speak to the actual casualty numbers with respect to the villages that were attacked. I am aware, obviously, that the 28th Division did attack various Bosnian Serb villages. His words are correct with the fact that it was the Bosnian Muslims who were responsible, to my knowledge, of the death of an UNPROFOR peacekeeper there, so that is accurate. And again, I -- to beat a dead horse on this issue, I've always agreed that the safe area was not demilitarised and that the 28th Division conducted combat operations out of it. I mean, it's that knowledge which gives me the foundation to say that, you know, the VRS was entitled to attack the 28th Infantry Division because it represented a military threat to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One last thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you again read the whole portion without any need to do that. If the witness would have read it, it would have been sufficient. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's no B/C/S of this one, so I think for purposes of the public and of getting it so that my client can understand it, I was entitled to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wasn't aware that there was no B/C/S version of that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at the next part: "Atrocities made over innocent civilians have resulted in an action of neutralising Muslim terrorists. Our activities are by no means directed against civilians or the UNPROFOR members being deployed in this enclave. This fact was obvious to a certain number of UNPROFOR members who went over to our territory after one of your soldiers had been killed by the Muslims. They have been accepted in a human way, well accommodated and secure." Based upon your research, are these words by General Mladic in accord with international law or are they criminal per se or unlawful per se as I think that the --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first -- could we first seek to establish whether what is written here reflects the events --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- before we enter into the next question, that is, whether they're in accord with international law or per se unlawful. Please proceed. Could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was my first thing. I mean, commenting on the facts, it is obviously factual that many of the UN soldiers did turn themselves over to the custody of the advancing Bosnian Serb forces because they believed it was safer than trying to withdraw through the ABiH military forces. They have been -- they were accepted. Obviously I am aware that at the point in time that NATO forces began bombing Bosnian Serb military forces on the afternoon of the 10th of July, that there was a threat made that if bombing operations resumed or continued by NATO, that the UNPROFOR people would be harmed. So essentially there is some information out there that would suggest that at some point they became potential hostages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were they physically harmed while in the custody of the VRS, such as to have there be any casualties?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, ultimately they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And focusing now on these words, do you find them in accord with what you would expect to be accepted behaviour of a military officer or do you find anything in these words to be unlawful per se?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. What words? There's a lot of words. It's vague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We had the words and we had the events. We tried to separate them. Could you please be very precise in putting that question to the witness, but perhaps we should do it after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we take the break first. We would like to see you back in 20 minutes, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, your time estimate would still --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir, the same time estimate. We're talking approximately, I would say, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 20 minutes after the break. Then I would like to put the following on the record. There was an issue about the translation -- or, rather, I should say the missing B/C/S translation of 65 ter 17957 which initially was MFI'd as D367. Now, a few things went wrong there uploaded -- having been uploaded the same document -- different documents under the same ERN number. As matters stand now, I -- D367 is admitted into evidence and the extraneous English version of the document, doc ID 0185-7879 can be removed and then everything should be okay again. Finally, the Defence has informed today - and I'm now talking about D361, so we're leaving D367 behind us - the Defence has informed that the English translation of D361 has been uploaded in e-court under ERN number 0449-7473-0449-7473-ET, and the Chamber has instructed the Registry to attach the translation but the Registry is unable to locate a document under the number as I just read out. And we do understand that the Defence will further look into that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I can actually respond now if it pleases the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is my understanding that that was a Prosecution 65 ter number. We have the document that the Prosecution provided as the translation uploaded as a 1D number, but I was told to ask whether we can link a Defence document with a Prosecution document or if that needs to be done by the Prosecution as a technical matter. Otherwise, my information is that we have now uploaded that so that if we are to link ours with the Prosecution document, it can be done and I can have my staff send the appropriate locator information, the 1D number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm informed that as long as you have uploaded it under a separate ID number, that then Madam Registrar is able to attach that document but it should be uploaded under a separate ID number. If that's done, then the problem is resolved. We'll hear from Madam Registrar after the break if that's not the case. We take a break and we'll resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness is escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Ivetic or Mr. Lukic, your exploring the 11 lines, has that resulted in any position?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we just spoke with Ms. Stewart. We are trying to locate those 11 lines and the connection we have to tie them with so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- Okay then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- we don't have any response --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're patiently waiting for the results of all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We left off with the third paragraph of the document that's before us and I'd simply like to focus my question on the words contained in that paragraph and ask you if this -- if you find them in accord with what you would expect to be the accepted behaviour of a military officer or do you find anything in these words to be unlawful per se?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, there -- looking at the language of the third paragraph, there is nothing that I would view as being patently unlawful in that language.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to D00150. This is dated the 4th of September, 1995, again from General Mladic --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. If we could then not broadcast the same. If we could turn to page 5 in both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to focus on the second-to-last paragraph in both. And ask you to read that to yourself, where he's talking about wishing to make a full contribution to the peace process, proposing to schedule an urgent meeting of commanders of the warring parties to sign a complete, lasting and unconditional cessation of hostilities on the territory of the former BH. And let me know, sir, when you've read that entire paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that General Mladic consistently sought and asked for the international community to help negotiate a cease-fire and peace across the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina from approximately 1993 onwards?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that, with respect to -- from 1993 onwards, given the fact that the Bosnian Serb side had achieved what they believed were their war aims, that there were a number of peace feelers going out from the political leadership. I don't -- I assumed that General Mladic would be party to that from the Bosnian Serb side, and certainly in this particular case, you know, given the context of September 1995, NATO aircraft are bombing the VRS and the Croatian army and the ABiH are jointly undertaking Operation Storm and the VRS is losing ground. Again, yes, I can see at this juncture why General Mladic would be requesting a broad cease-fire in order to stop the hostilities for that respect. So again, there were various -- the VRS and the ABiH -- I'm sorry, the RS, given the fact that they'd achieved their war aims from 1993 on, were looking to essentially end the war at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You mention NATO attacks and actions of the Croatian army and the ABiH in September 1995. Was there also action directly by UNPROFOR and the Rapid Reaction Force, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, the Rapid Reaction Force was NATO and not UNPROFOR. So I say -- when I put -- when I say "NATO," that's what I'm, you know, referring to. I don't believe the Rapid Reaction Force was subordinate to UNPROFOR. Again, I could be mistaken but that's not my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I told you that General Smith testified that he personally commanded over the RRF, would that change your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If General Smith says that, then that would -- you know, certainly if -- he is the UNPROFOR commander at the time, yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Irrespective of who commanded the RRF, did -- do you believe that during this time-period the military activities of the RRF, NATO aircraft, the Croat forces, and the ABiH were co-ordinated with one another?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would defer on that question because, one, it was not an area that I studied, it had nothing to do with Srebrenica 1995, and certainly there are much better people than I am to be able to have testified about that with respect to the overall co-ordination if any existed. It just was not an area that I needed to deal with for the area of my study of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. I'd now like to go through some recordings with you of Mr. Mladic. And first of all, did you have occasion to review in detail the so-called Srebrenica trial video as we refer to it in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen versions of Srebrenica trial videos in other cases. In this particular case, I don't know if it's the same version that I've seen or not, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. I just have some short clips I'd like to go through with you. With the assistance of Ms. Stewart on the opposite side, I'd like to show the first clip which is from 65 ter -- pardon me, Exhibit Number P1147 and is the video that is labelled V000-9265 and I'd ask for the section to be played from 00:43:09 to 00:45:54. And this is, I believe, approximately located at page 17 of the English transcript of this exhibit through page 18. And with that said, I'd like to play the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, first of all, sir, this clip that we've seen, is that one of the clips that you remember seeing for purposes of prior cases perhaps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did your research confirm that it was UNPROFOR rather than the VRS that initiated the decision that refugees would be evacuated from the area based on instructions from BH command and the requests of the refugees themselves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, what my research reflected is what Colonel Karremans was saying here, his perception that the refugees wanted to leave, and I think there are related documents from the BH command that discuss potentially moving the population out of Potocari. Again, the question of whose idea and under what circumstances is a matter of debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, who asked for this meeting according to Mr. -- Colonel Karremans?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans did ask for this meeting. This is what is known as the first meeting of the three that take place on the 11th -- I'm sorry, on the 10th and 11th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to now show another short clip, of 36 or so seconds, in the same video from 49 seconds and -- 49 minutes and 5 seconds to 49 minutes and 41 seconds, and again with the assistance of Ms. Stewart, who I thank very much for her assistance. And if we can play it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, this is part of the same clip so I won't ask you if you viewed it, but the reference by Mr. -- Colonel Karremans suggesting that they go towards Tuzla, is the ultimate direction in which the refugees were sent -- in the general direction of Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could now look at the same underlying video, and it's the part that begins at one hour, 33 minutes, and 41 seconds, and goes to one hour, 38 minutes, and 17 seconds, it's approximately three and a half minutes and I'd like to play that, that begins at page 41 of the English transcript and goes to page 42 of the English transcript. And again, with the assistance of Ms. Stewart, I'd like to play that at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in terms of the overall entirety of General Mladic's words, would you agree that he is promoting the option of a peaceful resolution, whereby the enemy force lays down its arms without further bloodshed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In the context of this, and this is the second meeting on 11 July, he is making the case essentially that if the 28th Division were to lay down their arms and surrender, they would be spared.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in this context at this time, the VRS still thought that the 28th Division was tied up in the Bandera Triangle, armed and waiting for them. Is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is there anything -- strike that. He seems to be seeking a meeting with political or military leaders and has proposed a cease-fire at 10.00 a.m. to permit that meeting to take place. Is there anything in --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. He ordered a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey objects against the way in which you quote what was said, or at least summarise what was said, it being that Mr. Mladic did not propose a cease-fire but ordered one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then please rephrase your question and put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General Mladic seems to be seeking a meeting with political and military leaders and has ordered a unilateral cease-fire at 10.00 a.m. for that purpose. Do you find anything patently unlawful in these words or are they, in fact, a typical message that you would expect a military commander to make after prevailing in a battle to try to avoid further fighting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you split that up, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a lot of questions in one. The first question apparently be whether there's anything patently unlawful in those words. Is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect to him ordering a cease-fire for the purpose of bringing in members of either the Muslim political establishment or the 28th Infantry Division to negotiate their surrender, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the words of General Mladic are, in fact, a typical message you would expect any military commander to make after prevailing in a battle to try to avoid further fighting?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we get the specific words, given what General Mladic has just said that's a -- quite a bit to bite off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, what specific part are you referring to when you ask this question? Are you just limiting yourself to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The requesting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- cease-fire and requesting a meeting? Is that what you --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, I would add to that also requesting that they surrender their arms, that the military surrender their arms, and reach a -- send negotiators to reach a peaceful resolution to the situation. Those are the words I'm referring to. I think we've all heard them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have heard many more, but if you are focusing on these ones, then the witness may answer the question -- unless Mr. McCloskey --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mr. Butler will concentrate on military terms, but if we could have the context by which that last one was said, survive or disappear. These are connected to what you just said and they should be mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is that a submission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you said you would limit yourself whether that is of any use is a different matter, but you would say just offering -- asking for a meeting, asking to surrender your weapons. And, Mr. Butler, you're supposed to forget about all the rest that was said --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, let's do the whole thing. Let's do it this way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Ivetic, that's the way you phrased it, that's where Mr. McCloskey made objections, and I denied that objection because you wanted to limit purely on those words and not on "survive" or "stay and vanish." You apparently have excluded that, fine; then that's your question. If you want to include it, do it then -- again rephrase your question and then we'll hear whether Mr. McCloskey has any further objection against the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, let's first start with the question Mr. McCloskey did not have an objection to or for rather I should say for which you overruled his objection. If we focus on the words of surrendering arms, sending prominent military or political people to negotiate a surrender, ordering a unilateral cease-fire to accomplish the same, in relation to those words, sir, are they the type of comments that you would expect to hear from any military officer from any army in a similar situation where they have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Similarity of the situation -- situation is not described, Mr. Ivetic. And there of course that's exactly where the problem is and sighing loudly doesn't change that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to proceed now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- proceed as you wish to proceed. Your -- the only thing is, if you say "in a similar situation," which you have not defined --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I did in my question, Your Honour, the one that you overruled the objection to. There is an objection, it is overruled, is that question then able to be introduced to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you introduced new elements in the question and that, even without an objection, would meet concerns by the Chamber as I expressed before. You've played a long portion of a video and you are referring to a similar situation which makes it entirely unclear. Proceed as you think fit to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. I'll proceed with the question that you said was appropriate and that's at page 59, 20 through to 24, where I precisely did identify the similar situation as being a military commander to make after prevailing in a battle to try to avoid further fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that -- could you answer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, in the technical sense that Srebrenica has just been captured, General Mladic is seeking the surrender of the 28th Division rather than to continue to engage them in battle, the fact that he would offer a cease-fire and the fact that he would make the necessary provisions to allow for those individuals to travel to, in this case the Hotel Fontana, to negotiate that surrender, I mean, that's all technically proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question please, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to the whole context of events where I believe you've testified that the VRS thought that the 28th Division was still in the Bandera Triangle, do you permit the possibility that his reference to they may vanish or not survive could be in relation to the population in the Bandera Triangle, military and civilian, engaging in hostile activities that he's expecting he will have to commit -- commit combat against?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. Anything is possible and this is not Mr. Butler's job to speculate on these sorts of Mladic comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would say the opposite. He's a military analyst who's here to tell us what the possible ramifications of words are based upon his knowledge of the facts of the area and I'm asking him now a very pertinent question, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may answer the question whether he considers it possible that those words have been uttered in relation to the people, military and civilians, in the Bandera Triangle, whether the context of all of it, whether he considered this a possibility.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, sir, that is a possible interpretation of that language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could have just one moment, Your Honours, to see what the consultation is behind my back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could Mr. Mladic keep his voice low so that no one else can hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise for the delay, Your Honours. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you done with the words and the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have told us, Mr. Butler, that this is a possible interpretation. Is it your interpretation of those words in that context? Or if you say I have no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, sir, in this particular context I -- I've never -- I've never analysed the words in the sense -- and again, trying to be conservative, what Mr. -- what General Mladic says is what he says. What he means is not something -- just like any of us, I don't interpret what people mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That's an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could now view -- and this is part of the -- another video within that same exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, not a surprise, I take it, that I'm surprised at this moment that you announced that you would need 20 minutes, where I'm not saying that only the video you played, but you had a lot of other questions, you started playing the video, and we are now approximately 15 minutes beyond your time estimate. But I just want you to be aware of going quite a bit beyond your last estimate. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And I can advise you that I only have two, or actually just the one more short video of approximately three minutes and one or two questions about that and then I'll be concluding my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can have the second -- pardon me -- the video in question now is V000-9266 and it is the segment from 9 minutes and 54 seconds to 12 minutes and 50 seconds. And it can be found on page 49 of the English transcript for this exhibit and again with Ms. Stewart's assistance we can begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in the -- in this clip, again there is the request for the surrender of arms so that the husbands, fathers, and neighbours don't need to die and the one woman says: How do we contact them? Would you agree, under the circumstances, that it is just as likely that they're referring to the 28th Division, that is again to be believed in the Bandera Triangle holed up, that these comments are directed towards?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again, that's a possible interpretation that they're referring to the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be the last question I have for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I thank you for the time and I apologise for going over my estimate by a dozen or so minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. McCloskey, any questions in re-examination for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed. Could you give us a time estimate? I'm not asking for seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I hope to finish today, though that last section and the Ministry of Defence part about the judicial system did open the doors up, but I really do want to finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, just on this last section when the General said on the night of the 11th that he ordered a cease-fire until 10.00, are you aware of evidence of an assault by troops under General Mladic's command on the enclave of specifically Potocari that came from the Bratunac area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Starting at -- on the morning of the 12th, as the documents indicate, the special police forces began moving from Bratunac to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when General Mladic said he ordered a cease-fire until 10.00 a.m., that was not correct, was it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, as the record notes with respect to the intercepts and everything else, I mean there was fighting throughout the night of the 10th as the first part of the column started to break its way through the enclave. So, I mean, certainly -- or not -- through the northern edge of the former enclave. So they weren't aware that -- if this was a cease-fire, it was a broader one. You know, and it's certainly from the context of the special police, I mean, they weren't necessarily firing their weapons, but certainly they were conducting military operations towards Potocari. Presumably they would have fired the weapons had they been fired upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, in the context of what General Mladic said at least twice, that it was Muslim options to survive or disappear and for their survival their army must lay down their weapons, and did the entire 28th Division, in fact, lay down their weapons or did they, as you've described, push forward in combat fashion all the way up towards Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 28th Division did, in fact, attempt to leave the enclave and try to push towards, what they considered, friendly territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if General Mladic is offering for their survival, they must surrender, they didn't surrender and the option of -- and the next option was disappearing or vanishing --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what happened --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Misstates the evidence and calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The misstatement of the evidence always is an issue which -- could you please be as precise as possible. But could you assist us, Mr. Ivetic, is it the next option -- if you just quote the words to the witness, that would be preferable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Mladic said -- gave the option twice, they may survive or vanish. Then he said: For your survival, and then I paraphrase, your men must surrender. Now, as you've just stated, a good part of the 28th Division did not surrender. So does it make sense to you, Mr. Butler, that having not followed General Mladic's edict or comments, that the Muslims, by ignoring his comments, faced the other option that he gave and that is vanishment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again I would object since we've established there's an alternate meaning under those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, we agreed that he's speaking of the 28th Division --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, what the meaning of the words is let's focus to what was said. It's my recollection that in the first one the option was stay -- at least is what the last words -- I want to have them played again if -- I don't want any further discussion. Words are to be quoted literally and that can be the basis of a question and the witness already said that he was not -- he was not explaining those words. He says words are what they are and that's of course what the Chamber will primarily consider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the first one was "survive or stay and vanish." I think those were the words I remember having read on the subtitles. The second time it was "survive or disappear" and for survival it was required that they would lay down their weapons. That is my recollection of the two portions we looked at. That is, if the parties agree on that, that is then the basis for any further questions without further interpretation of what it means or whether it was -- that's the basis for your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I think given Mr. Butler's reluctance to take over your job and this is clear, we don't need to spend any more time with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Mr. Butler said words are words. I'm not the one who should explain them. Therefore, let's move on. The Chamber may have to explain them perhaps at one stage sooner or later. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, the -- you spoke at length about intercepts and, as I recollect, and on cross-examination you mostly have mentioned the 2nd Corps intercepts. As part of your review of all these intercepts, did that include MUP intercepts, Ministry of Interior intercepts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe that we had intercepts that -- as part of that general body came out of very -- the CSB in Tuzla which we called a subset which was the MUP intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And without going into a lot of detail about that, did your -- did you gain a certain faith in those intercepts as you did with the others and actually cite them in your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, in fact, I believe the 12th July intercept where Mladic makes the remark about - and I apologise, I don't have the exact words - that people -- that they've all evacuated and we'll evacuate -- excuse me, they've all surrendered and that we'll evacuate all of them, those that want to and those that don't want to, that was, in fact, a MUP intercept. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And also Mr. Ivetic spent some time on September 11th speaking of around 16500 onward about -- that you never mentioned the constitution of the RS or the SFRY in your discussions of the law. And so I'd like to go briefly to some of the materials that you did discuss in your -- in particular, I believe it was in your command reports. If we could go to 65 ter 4384. We see this section that it's from the Official Gazette of the Republika Srpska dated 9 August 1993, Law on Amending the Criminal Code of the SFRY. What is this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What this document is, essentially, is a decree published in the Official Gazette of the RS where the Republika Srpska is essentially adopting almost, with minor changes, the former criminal code of the SFRY and directing that, you know, it be enforced as the criminal code, you know, retitled and enforced as the criminal code of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04384 receives number P2182, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. But could we just first have a look at how long it is, what are we looking at? It is -- by the way it said it is a decree -- the title reads that it is a law and it's three pages I see. Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right can we go to 65 ter 4379.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is this the criminal code that was referred to in that -- in the gazette that got adopted by the RS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to e-court page 69, B/C/S page 66. And we see here that this is chapter 16 of that law; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you chosen these and cited these in your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe they were pertinent with respect to the issue of command responsibility, so I did examine these and they are cited in my various command reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we can see that there's a genocide article, war crimes against the civilian population, it goes on to talk about war crimes against the sick and war crimes against prisoners of war, is that right, and others?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The whole quote or is there -- just in order for us to learn that there was a genocide and war crimes against the civilian population article in the former code. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any disagreement about any of the questions you've asked? Mr. Ivetic, any disagreement about genocide article?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, no disagreement over that, although the B/C/S has some handwriting, I don't know what that is in relation to but I don't think it changes the meaning of the printed text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, 129 pages for the Judges to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry that we've done that. I just wanted chapter 16 which has basically the applicable statutes that Mr. Butler is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then please upload them. May I take it that there is no --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. So if you upload them, they will be admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can we have 65 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we could already provisionally assign a number to what is still to be uploaded as chapter 6 -- 16 of the criminal code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document with 65 ter number pending to be provided receives number P2183, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that number is reserved. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll assign it 4379A. And if we could go to 65 ter 4646, this should be another order from the gazette of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, this one dated 13 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see here, Mr. Butler, that this is an order on something called the application of the rules of the international law of war in the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia Herzegovina. And we can read to ourselves what this does. Tell us briefly what this is, why it was in your report.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. One of the documents that I use in my report is the former SFRY regulations pertaining to the application of the law of war or international -- or law -- or international humanitarian law, I guess, with respect to the armed forces of the Republika Srpska. This particular order by Dr. Karadzic, functioning as the supreme commander, I mean, essentially lays out the fact that those 1988 regulations, with respect to how to follow the law of armed conflict within the military, are applicable to what becomes the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04646 receives number P2184, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go to 65 ter 4377. I'm not sure how we got that. Maybe if we go to the next page in the B/C/S. It should be page 2 in e-court. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are these the JNA regs that were just talked about and were adopted by the RS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, these are the former regulations that were made applicable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would like to go to -- should be page 62 in the English and B/C/S page 56. And I want to ask you about -- it's the bottom part, basic rights of prisoners of war, number 207 is entitled: "Responsibility of the State for the treatment of prisoners of war by its nationals." And "prisoners of war are under the authority of the Detaining Power, and not of the individual persons or military units which capture them. The Detaining Power shall be responsible for the treatment of prisoners of war. This responsibility does not rule out ... personal responsibility of individuals." It is break time, but, Mr. Butler, I think you can give us your brief analysis of why you've used this and do you view it as important?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have used it. I view it as important as part of a component of the responsibility of the state and the senior leaders of the state to ensure the proper treatment of prisoners of war. The fact that in other trials some defendants have claimed that it, you know, since they were captured by unit X, that their -- the problem of that particular unit that captures them, and again, this lays out that under the regulations that were applicable to them, the VRS being "them," that they understood from these regulations that, you know, the senior leaders of the state, whatever organ they are, share responsibility because it's not an individual who deals with the -- is responsible for ensuring the fair treatment of prisoners, it's the state as the detaining power.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see that it also, at the end, says this responsibility does not rule out personal responsibility of individuals. What do you take that to mean briefly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That an individual, any member of that unit X, so to speak, if they commit a crime against a prisoner, they can't simply claim that it's the state's responsibility. I mean, as designed there's a two-tiered level of responsibility: Those individuals obviously who are directly responsible for the capture, maintenance, and movement of a prisoner, as well as the overarching state to ensure that all of the proper procedures are filled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's break time. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While the witness is escorted into the courtroom, it turns out that everything in relation to D361 is now correct, has been correctly uploaded, has been attached. Therefore, D361 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I also have some additional information as to the witness. You asked about the 92 bis I believe witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- Music I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- is the name of the witness. We have located the transcript portion. We do not have an objection to those additional lines being brought in, but we would renew our objection to have -- and our request to have this witness cross-examined insofar as the lines now being added relate to a contradiction between the written statement and the testimony of the witness during the trial that we believe still needs to be further explored and clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so I don't know whether this is -- I forgot if this is one where Your Honours have already ruled on our objections --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there is a decision already. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if the additional lines, the 11 lines really would change anything not covered by your objections yet and therefore not by the ruling of the Chamber, then, of course, you are invited to make any specific submission. But if you say, We are opposed to it in general terms but not in any different way for these 11 lines, then we leave it as it is and we would then also admit those 11 lines. We'd like to hear from you soon. Mr. McCloskey, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, while we're here we see in -- up on the page 209 entitled: "Prohibition of reprisals." And it notes that: "Reprisals against prisoners of war are prohibited in all cases." What is a reprisal in a military context as you would have learned?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A reprisal is a deliberate decision to essentially commit a war crime for the specific purpose of essentially seeking to deter your adversary who's committing war crimes. It's -- like I said, it is something that occurs in extreme situations. Obviously there's a large body of international law that reflects that reprisals are inherently unlawful because you're essentially always targeting a protected population by doing so. I am aware some countries still believe that reprisals are, in fact, not necessarily lawful but still appropriate in some cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just briefly, 216, we note that it just talks about the personal belongings of prisoners of war and that in the middle of the paragraph we see that they shall remain in the possession of the prisoner of war, and early on it talks about clothing, food, identity cards, personal correspondence. Is this something you were aware of when you wrote your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I was aware of the requirement that military forces who capture prisoners, you know, again under this paragraph this is what they have to leave the prisoner with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I offer this document in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 48 -- 84 pages, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any disagreement about this being part of the law?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do we need the details of that, Mr. McCloskey, or is it just making reference to that reprisals and with the answer of the witness is sufficient for us to know, apart from that, of course, it's -- legal matters, of course, the Court could look into them itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: These are the key pages that I think we're satisfied and, of course, the Trial Chamber can -- will request, as I know it will, if it needs anything else, so I think these few pages we're fine with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we'll sort that out so we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Make your selection and then we'll reserve a number for it. Madam Registrar, the still-to-be-made selection of articles defining war crimes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document with the 65 ter number then to be provided receives tentatively number P2185, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is reserved for this purpose. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now I'd like to briefly go into the area that Defence went with you on directive 4 on Friday, September the 13th, from 16753 to 16761 and other areas and that is related to directive 4. And I want to first make a reference to a map that came from the Zvornik Brigade. Its number is 19292. I believe it's too big to actually come up on the screen and it -- I do have a blow-up section that should come up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I've been able to show the map to Mr. Ivetic and just to give the witness and you an idea of -- this is the original map that I'll have a blow-up for. It's a map that is from the Zvornik Brigade and it has a notation of -- Proboj is the name of the operation on it. If we could go to 19292A and just -- and blow that up. It's -- it's not a very good blow-up, as we can see. That's the -- I'm sorry, that's the whole map so that -- thank you for that. And I would -- then if we can go to now 19292A --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could -- apparently Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is no 19292A. It's only ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's been released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may take a short time to make it to Madam Registrar --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- electronically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and it seems -- but could -- Mr. Lukic, it seems that Mr. Mladic would like to have a look at the map, or at least he's gesturing one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. That was the message that was relayed. I don't know whether we have full-sized copies of this map available. I do not recall having received any, although I did just look at it laid out on the floor at the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The General can have the original as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Temporarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, temporarily, we understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, do you recall having had a chance to see any of the original or copies of the Operation Proboj maps from the Zvornik collection?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that when we went through the Zvornik documents that there were a number of maps there. I would have looked at all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, this now is up on the screen. It is a blow-up graphic of that original, and we can see that we have red lines and blue lines starting below Zvornik and in the area of Bratunac. You talked in your discussion on this about a pocket, basically, that was surrounded and is this roughly the area that you would have been talking about from -- we see that this is dated 24 -- it says beginning at 24 January 1993 and there is nothing in the ending section and if we go to the top we'll see that. Is this the area that was in contention after -- during that period of directive 4 from late 1992 until the creation of the enclave in the spring of 1993?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it would have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer both these maps into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar. "Both" means the total map and the portion taken out?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, please. One -- the map 19292 and then it's section 19292A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document number 19292 receives number P2186, and document 19292A receives number P2187, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2186 and P2187 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we go to 65 ter 14122. And if we could assist, we might save some time, I have a few of these documents that I will be going over that I would like Mr. Butler to see because it will save time in terms of looking at each page on the computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Defence aware of what is contained in the binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, but they are welcome to look and it's material that had been previously provided to them and I think largely discussed in most of the past Srebrenica trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It appears to be primarily information reports and proofing of the witness and some e-mails.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this first one, Mr. Butler, we see it's listed from the Drina Corps command 19 November 1992. It's the last page, on page 4 of the English, is -- we note that it's General Zivanovic's signature and that's -- or his name in any event, and that's on page 2 of the B/C/S. And I just want to focus on this first page. We see that this is 19 November. This is about the period that directive 4 came out, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we note that there's a mention of Cerska, Konjevic Polje, Glodansko Brdo, Kamenica, Snagovo. Are those some of the areas noted in directive 4 and the follow-up from the Drina Corps on directive 4?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the next paragraph we see it talks about the figure. "In addition to armed soldiers, there are a certain number of civilians (women, children, the elderly and the frail) in this area. We estimate this figure to be between 10.000 and 20.000 people." Is that a reliable figure in your view, based on your knowledge of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is -- I think it's towards the 20.000, but yes, sir, it is when you look at the context of the people who then showed up in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then page 2 of the English, B/C/S page 1. And we see that -- it says: "The morale of the civilians is dropping due to shortages of food staples and other vital supplies. We deem that we will crash the enemy resistance in a powerful attack precisely because of their drop in morale caused by joint attacks from all directions." Is this a roughly accurate picture as you've seen from the documents and about this time of the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is with respect to November and, of course, as you turn the corner through December and January particularly, it was that -- the winter of 1993 was a particularly harsh winter with a lot of snow in Eastern Bosnia. So there -- they were having all sorts of problems with respect to getting enough supplies or food in. So you see the situation continue to get worse with respect to the basic necessities of food and firewood and things of that nature as each month goes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I offer that document in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 14122 receives number P2188, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 65 ter 04021, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we'll see that this is an order from General Mladic that's dated the 7th of December, 1992. There we go. And it's an order to amend directive number 4 that speaks for itself. And then we see the -- just the first sentence, it says: "That all targeted objectives of the Army of Republika Srpska must be achieved ... by 13 December 1992 at the latest." And if we could go to the next page. Sorry to make you read this quickly, Mr. Butler. It should be B/C/S page 3. And we see that it says: "For this purpose, the goals and tasks set out in directive 4 ... November 1992 are to be completed by that date. "Despite the stages formerly set out in directive number 4, the Corps Commands must carry out the following assignments in their zones of responsibility by 13 December ..." And then in number 2 we see: "Liberate Orasje, Trnovo, Konjevic Polje, Cerska, and Teocak." Are the sections Konjevic Polje and Cerska the parts that were in the Drina Corps version of directive 4 that Zivanovic sent out?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'd offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is a translation issue on the first page. I believe in item number 1 "ciljevi rata" has not been translated. It's not target objectives, it's war objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll check that out and get an agreement and fix that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, the number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04021 receives number P2189, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think the best would be to mark it for identification so that you agree and then come back to the Chamber. It's marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we now go to 65 ter 14062.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we'll see that this is an order for combat dated 21 March 1993. It's from the Drina Corps and it's in the name of General Zivanovic and it's -- we can see here on the first page that it's to the commands of the Zvornik Brigade and the Birac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 3 in the English and it should be B/C/S page 2 and 3 ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can assist, I think there's only two pages in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. There should be another page in the B/C/S because there's another paragraph, I think, but -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In any event, if we could look at paragraph 2. "In accordance with the assignments specified in directive number 4 with addenda, the main forces of the Drina Corps are to continue conducting combat operations in the zone of the Tactical Group Visegrad and the operation aimed at liberating Srebrenica and Zepa ..." And what does this show us about the Drina Corps's objective regarding this issue and can you relate this to directive 4?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It shows that it hadn't changed yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 14062 receives number P2190, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2190 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 09540.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, as you'll see, we've now got a document from the Zvornik Brigade in the name of Vinko Pandurevic. I believe it's dated 31 January 1993, entitled: "Report on an unusual incident." I won't read it all, but we can see that around 2400 hours, a mixed column made up of women, children, and armed men from a certain direction fell into an ambush in Crni Vrh sector. The column which numbered about a hundred persons was fired on and dispersed and disappeared from the sector. Was this the kind of activity that you read about as you reviewed the materials related to the events after directive 4?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 09540 receives number P2191, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can we go to 65 ter 20872.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, this is an intercept dated in the Serbian or the -- excuse me, the B/C/S as 6 February 1993 that didn't get in the English translation. And we see that it's from Zivanovic and Gaborovic. And we see a mention of -- Zivanovic is saying: "Are the Turks' houses burning?" Gaborovic says: "They are burning, they are burning." Zivanovic says: "Way to go, as many as possible." Who could this Zivanovic be in this context on this date?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be the corps commander, I believe he's a general at this point, General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And from the content of this, does this appear to be related to the pocket that we talked about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would because the Kosoric that they're discussing is, I believe, the commander of the Milici or the Vlasenica Brigade which would have part of the responsibility for the western side of that pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We would object based upon our objections to the intercepts. I can't see right now the source if there's any additional objections, but I believe this is still in relation to the ABiH intercepts for which we've made our case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can't see it on the basis of all this, where it comes from, to what extent any of the objections are applicable to this one as well. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is not part of the standard collection that we got, so we can provide that information and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll mark it for identification at this moment and we'll further hear where it comes from. Madam Registrar, the number would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 20872 receives number P2192, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go to 65 ter 09134.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, this is from the command of the 1st Birac Light Infantry Brigade under the commander Svetozar Andric. Can you tell us, was the Birac Brigade involved in these orders related to directive 4?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And calling your attention to paragraph 2, we note that it's: "Our forces which are moving in the wider area of Kamenica, Gajici, and Grobici worked according to plan without major problems. The village of Gobelji has been burnt, and tomorrow the plan is to do Paljevine." Is this consistent with the -- some of the activity that you reviewed as you went through these kinds of documents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 09134 receives number P2193, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we have 65 ter number 9059.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is of a similar date, 10 March, Mr. Butler. It's a supplement to a regular combat report to the Drina Corps, this time from the familiar Vinko Pandurevic. He's talking about various terrain, we can see, in the Drinjaca river canyon. I won't go into all of that, but is that the area that was involved in the battle for the pocket that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, you look at these locations, they would -- they're in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The last line of that report: "We propose that the houses should not be torched when taking control of Konjevic Polje, but that they be inhabited by people from Tuzla and other areas." Who do you -- who is he talking about inhabiting these houses in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the common practices that all the parties would do is when various individuals got displaced from an area, in this particular context they're talking about Bosnian Serbs displaced from territory under the control of either the Bosnian Muslim or Croat side, is that they would place them in the houses of individuals from their regions that they displaced. So in this particular context, you know, the presumption here that I'm making is that Konjevic Polje is predominantly still a Muslim-population town. Once they displace that population, rather than burn the houses, leave the houses intact, and that they will populate them, then, with Bosnian Serbs who had been displaced from other areas of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was Pandurevic's unit, the Zvornik Brigade, working anywhere near Andric's unit, the Birac Brigade, in this operation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They were all working in concert on the northern end -- northern side of the pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 09059 receives number P2194, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: A last document on this topic, 65 ter 1088.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we'll soon see that this is an order marked "urgent" from General Mladic, dated the 10th of February, 1993. Do your best to read that and we noted that he's talking about the area of Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and Srebrenica and that he concludes in that first line that they're in a hopeless situation. And then the order is to start preparing per this task. And if we go to the next page, we get a little more an idea of this. Is this General Mladic's -- does this order have anything to do with the operations in the pocket that we've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And again, going back to the Defence's point about, you know, mixing between strategic and operational activities, you know, here you have General Mladic directing, you know, the 1st Krajina Corps to create a unit to send to the assistance of the Drina Corps for their combat activities, it shows the level of involvement that the Main Staff was in with respect to, you know, combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At least on critical parts of the battle-field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer that document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 01088 receives number P2195, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we go to D365. Mr. President, I found this under my pile. You had asked us to look into the January 1995 issue where an MSF was in trouble for smuggling something into the enclave, and so I would just call our attention to D365 to refresh our recollection on that. It's that paragraph at the bottom of the page. I won't read it, but we can see that someone named Jean or Jean, depending on his nationality, or hers, was removed for doing some sort of smuggling. If we could now go to D299. And that document was 11 January 1995 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we start rushing, Mr. Ivetic, would you have any questions in -- as matters stand now because it's a quarter past 2.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If so, then perhaps we better finish tomorrow morning. That's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I do, it would only be a handful, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I do have questions, it would only be a handful. Nothing significant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A handful is --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you still need, Mr. McCloskey, because we can't just rush through everything. If it is a matter of five, six, or seven minutes, fine, but if it is more -- then we still would need the co-operation by all those assisting us. But ... how many more documents do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's just one document that clears up this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let's -- could that be, if we read that document, would we know what was smuggled and what -- okay, then do we have to -- could the parties not agree that we receive that information by looking at that document from the bar table?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless there's anything specific this witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You'll see that he was smuggling in plumbing tools and some plumbing equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is clear. I think it is in evidence already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I remember that it was not -- not -- okay. And then you have one more document or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I had the -- somewhat -- of the four documents that answered your question about the agreement that General Mladic referred to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- and my preference is always probably 10 to 15 minutes of Mr. Butler's testimony as opposed to the work going into a bar table motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see the point. Let's -- we'll deal with it tomorrow. Let's not try to -- then you would need another 15 minutes tomorrow, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we've got to get it done in 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, 15 minutes. You know how many seconds that is?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm going to add them up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's 900. Mr. Butler, I give you the same instructions as I did before - you know them by heart - meanwhile not to communicate in any way with whoever about your testimony. We would like to see you back tomorrow morning for a last 900 seconds of examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. One quick question on this binder that was given by Mr. McCloskey, do I take this with me or do I return it to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Mr. McCloskey would like to have it back. He's gathering all his belongings, including maps. Then, Mr. Butler, we'd like to see you back but then for the last time --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- tomorrow morning at 9.30 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in this same courtroom. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 17th of September, at 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 17th day of September, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.
